name: Bangladesh
summary_text: Bangladesh is a dangerous destination for trans visitors, with escalating Islamist violence since the August 2024 political crisis that ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. Trans activist Shila was brutally murdered in February 2025 (police suspect extremist involvement). A human-rights group documented 260 anti-LGBTQI+ incidents in 2024 — including murder, arson, and blackmail — describing attacks as having "skyrocketed." Islamist fundamentalist groups have intensified attacks under the interim government, and LGBTQ+ people have been "forced into hiding." A mob stormed the gate of a safe house for third-gender people (one survivor said "I escaped only with my life"). Police extort hijra/trans people — dozens were arrested for refusing to pay extortion money, and five were arrested at Dhaka's international airport. The US State Department rates Bangladesh as Level 3 (Reconsider Travel).

sources.title: Bangladesh trans activist brutally murdered
sources.claim_summary: Erasing 76 Crimes (Feb 2025): prominent trans activist Shila was brutally murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district on 3 February 2025; police suspect extremists due to the nature of the attack. She was known for advocating legal recognition, healthcare access and safe spaces. JusticeMakers Bangladesh in France (JMBF) condemned the murder and called for legal reform.

sources.title: Bangladesh grows even more dangerous for its LGBTQI+ citizens
sources.claim_summary: Erasing 76 Crimes (April 2026): JMBF's annual report on 2025 documented 260 incidents of human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals in Bangladesh - a sharp increase continuing an upward trend since 2022 - including murder, arson and blackmail, with the interim government failing to protect them. Section 377 criminalises same-sex relations; the 2013 hijra recognition policy has not translated into effective protection or equal access to employment, healthcare, justice or services.

sources.title: No Longer Safe: Extremism Upends Trans Lives in Bangladesh
sources.claim_summary: Global Press Journal feature: after the 2024 Monsoon Revolution, rising conservative Islamist influence has upended trans and third-gender lives in Dhaka - a mob stormed a third-gender safe house, community leaders went into hiding, and trans people are retreating from public life and erasing identities they once displayed openly. Notes third-gender recognition since 2013 and a trans woman elected mayor of a rural town in 2021.

sources.title: LGBTQ Bangladeshis increasingly vulnerable a year after government toppled
sources.claim_summary: Washington Blade (Aug 2025): 'LGBTQ Bangladeshis increasingly vulnerable a year after government toppled' — threats and attacks rise amid Islamist mobilisation and collapsing protections.

sources.title: Country policy and information note: sexual orientation and gender identity, Bangladesh, April 2026 (accessible) - GOV.UK
sources.claim_summary: UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity in Bangladesh (updated April 2026): official UK asylum guidance assessing the legal position (Section 377), the hijra third-gender recognition, societal treatment, state protection levels, and risk to LGBT individuals - detailed country-of-origin information.

sources.title: Bangladesh | Outright International
sources.claim_summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): the 1860 Penal Code outlaws 'intercourse against the order of nature' with up to life imprisonment; rarely enforced but used by police as a pretext to harass perceived LGBTIQ people. Hijra people have been legally recognised as a third gender since 2014. Islamist groups have become vocal opponents - a BRAC University professor publicly tore a school textbook containing a transgender character, sparking backlash against gender diversity.

sources.title: Bangladesh police arrest dozens of third-gender people
sources.claim_summary: Erasing 76 Crimes (Oct 2025): dozens of hijras arbitrarily arrested across Bangladesh after refusing to pay extortion money to police, per JMBF. In Chattogram, at least twelve hijras were injured in an assault after filing a police complaint; in Narayanganj, twelve hijras were arrested while collecting money from vehicles - a traditional livelihood. JMBF alleges false extortion cases.

sources.title: Bangladesh: 5 trans women arrested for begging
sources.claim_summary: Erasing 76 Crimes (April 2024): five trans/hijra women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to one month by a mobile court for 'extortion' and 'public disturbance'. JMBF condemned the convictions as exacerbating marginalisation of an already vulnerable group.

sources.title: Tribunal decisions
sources.claim_summary: UK Upper Tribunal (Immigration and Asylum Chamber) decision PA/07096/2017 (Feb 2019): a Bangladeshi gay man's asylum appeal - the Home Office accepted Section 377 criminalises same-sex activity but argued it is not fully enforced; the decision examines country evidence on risk to gay men in Bangladesh - detailed case-law assessment of the actual risk profile.
